reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Acute traumatic tears follow a twisting injury on a loaded flexed knee, often in younger athletes
Degenerate tears occur in older knees, frequently with osteoarthritis, and may have minimal trauma
Symptoms include joint-line pain, effusion, catching or locking, and a sense of giving way
True locking (a fixed block to extension) suggests a displaced bucket-handle fragment
Joint-line tenderness with positive McMurray or Thessaly tests supports the diagnosis
Only the peripheral (red) zone has a blood supply, so peripheral tears can be repaired whereas central tears are usually debrided
In degenerate tears with osteoarthritis, exercise therapy is generally preferred to arthroscopic meniscectomy
reference.pathophysiology: The menisci are fibrocartilaginous shock absorbers that distribute load and stabilise the knee. Shear and compressive forces on a rotating flexed knee, or cumulative degeneration, tear the collagen architecture in vertical, horizontal, radial, flap or bucket-handle patterns. Because only the outer third is vascularised, healing potential depends on tear location; loss of meniscal function increases contact stress and accelerates cartilage degeneration.
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing radiographs to assess osteoarthritis and alignment
MRI of the knee as the primary imaging test
Diagnostic arthroscopy where imaging is equivocal and mechanical symptoms persist
Aspiration if a tense effusion or haemarthrosis needs characterisation
redFlags: A truly locked knee that cannot fully extend
Tense haemarthrosis suggesting associated ligament or osteochondral injury
Signs of septic arthritis (hot swollen knee with fever) mimicking a mechanical effusion
reference.prognosis: Peripheral repairable tears in stable knees heal well; degenerate tears often improve with rehabilitation, and outcomes after meniscectomy are limited by the long-term risk of accelerated osteoarthritis, especially with larger resections.
pitfalls: Recommending arthroscopic meniscectomy for degenerate tears with established osteoarthritis
Missing an associated ACL rupture in an acute haemarthrosis
Interpreting incidental MRI meniscal signal as the pain source in older patients
Overlooking a reducible bucket-handle tear as the cause of a locked knee
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
